notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 57 from the sources below. A few gaps up front: I didn't find any real disagreement between Protestant denominations on this psalm. The sources mostly agree on the plain meaning, and the main split is between historical readings and readings that apply the psalm to Christ. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm on the allowed sites, so those are left out.

---

**Title (Do Not Destroy / Miktam / the cave)**
- **Traditional:** Kidner thinks "Do Not Destroy" is probably the name of a tune, comparing Isaiah 65:8. He also points to David's order about Saul in 1 Samuel 26:9. Guzik thinks the cave was probably Adullam (1 Sam 22:1), though En Gedi (1 Sam 24) is possible. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/
- Spurgeon counts four "Destroy not" psalms (57, 58, 59, 75). He notes that David said "destroy not" about Saul and now prays the same words to God. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps057.php
- Clarke links the psalm to the cave at En Gedi. He suggests "Destroy not!" was God's warning to David when Saul was in his power. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/57-1.html
- Matthew Henry gives two readings: David refusing to destroy Saul, or God not letting David be destroyed, "for a blessing is in him," even Christ. Same URL.
- Ellicott takes Al-taschith as the opening words of a song whose tune was used. He sees the psalm as built partly from older hymns, and notes that its second half was reused in Psalm 108. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/57.htm
- Gotquestions says "Do Not Destroy" probably named a melody or musical style, and that scholars dispute what *miktam* means. https://www.gotquestions.org/Do-Not-Destroy.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET notes):** "Do not destroy" may be a style of music, a tune or an instrument. The meaning of *miktam* is uncertain, and one standard Hebrew dictionary (HALOT) gives "inscription." The cave is probably the one in 1 Sam 22:1 or 24:3. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psa+57%3A1&theme=false
- **Catholic (Augustine):** He reads the psalm as being about Christ's Passion. The "title" that was not to be corrupted is the sign "King of the Jews" on the cross, which Pilate refused to change. The cave stands for Christ hiding his Godhead in human flesh, and also for his rock-cut tomb. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801057.htm

**v. 1**
- **Traditional:** Spurgeon says the doubled cry shows how urgent the need is. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps057.php
- Guzik says David's trust doesn't earn mercy; it tells God he is David's only hope. The "wings" picture is a mother bird sheltering her chicks (compare Matthew 23:37). Boice adds that David calls God his refuge, not the cave. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/
- Poole: David trusts God's protection, not the dark cave, and expects the troubles to end soon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/57-1.htm
- Ellicott: "trusteth" is better translated "has taken refuge," and "danger of destruction" fits the Hebrew better than "calamities." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/57.htm
- Pulpit traces the wings image back to Deuteronomy 32:11. https://biblehub.com/psalms/57-1.htm
- **NET:** The Hebrew verb tense suggests a finished act of taking shelter that still holds. The wings picture God as a protective mother bird. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psa+57%3A1&theme=false
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Christ speaks this prayer as a man. The words about the shadow of the wings are also the Church's voice, waiting until wrongdoing has passed. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801057.htm

**v. 2**
- **Traditional:** Spurgeon notes that the KJV translators added "all things" because the Hebrew leaves a blank, like a blank cheque. Whatever God starts, he finishes. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps057.php
- JFB: God "completes what He has begun." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_057.cfm
- Ellicott: the Hebrew literally says "completes for me" (compare Ps 138:8). The Greek (LXX) and Latin (Vulgate) translations read "my benefactor," from a slightly different Hebrew word, and Ellicott leans toward that reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/57.htm
- Pulpit: the title "Elohim Elyon" (God Most High) appears only here and in Ps 78:56. https://biblehub.com/psalms/57-2.htm
- Kidner says "God Most High" may recall God's care for Abram, another homeless man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Following the "benefactor" reading, he takes past kindness as grounds for confidence. The greatest kindness is sending Christ. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801057.htm

**v. 3**
- **Traditional:** Ellicott: the Selah in mid-verse seems out of place (the LXX puts it after v. 2), and "reproach" here means "rebuke." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/57.htm
- Maclaren thinks this Selah highlights the enemy's wickedness, matching the Selah in v. 6 that highlights his ruin. Clarke says that if there were no human help, God would send angels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/
- JFB: mercy and truth are pictured as messengers sent to rescue. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_057.cfm
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon says that when we send prayers up, God sends help down, but David prays as well as trusts. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps057.php
- **Catholic (Augustine):** The Father "sent from heaven" in raising Christ. Christ himself is the mercy and truth that were sent. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801057.htm
- Augustine also applies "those who trample me" to the Jewish people, saying they were scattered and now carry the Scriptures that witness to Christ. That is his historical reading and should be presented as such. Same URL.

**v. 4**
- **Traditional:** Spurgeon pictures Saul's men as lions roaring around the cave. He says it is a triumph of faith to lie down among firebrands and rest. The tongue is called "sharp" but the teeth are not, as if words wound worse than teeth. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps057.php
- Venema (quoted by Spurgeon) says the key word "I will lie down" suggests calm security, like Ps 3:5 and 4:8. Same URL.
- Ellicott: "set on fire" is better translated "greedy ones" (literally "lickers"), describing the lions. The picture is of going to sleep each night surrounded by danger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/57.htm
- Matthew Henry: these are beasts of prey in human shape, and a spiteful tongue is Satan's weapon. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_057.cfm
- Guzik links the lions to 1 Peter 5:8. He lists Spurgeon's comforts, including that God keeps the lions on a leash and that there is another Lion, of Judah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/
- Spurgeon also urges asking for grace to stay among the "lions" and seek to save them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-57.html
- **Christ-centred reading:** One reading quoted by Spurgeon applies the verse to the Church: the devil is the roaring lion, and our sins are lion cubs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-57.html
- John Boys applies it to Christ's enemies shouting "Crucify him." https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps057.php
- Augustine likewise says the enemies' tongues killed Christ through that shout. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801057.htm

**v. 5 (refrain)**
- **Traditional:** Benson: in his distress David didn't pray "exalt me" but "exalt your own name." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/57-5.htm
- Barnes: David's first wish is not his own safety but God's honour. Same URL.
- Gill notes the Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) reads "above the angels of heaven." Pulpit explains it as God showing his might so the angels watch. Same URL.
- Boice: David wants God exalted in his own personal circumstances. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/
- **Catholic (Augustine):** The verse contrasts the man on the cross with God above the heavens. He argues the verse is fulfilled in the worldwide Catholic Church, against the Donatist schism of his day. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801057.htm

**v. 6**
- **Traditional:** Spurgeon: the pits hunters dug were placed on the animal's usual path ("before me"). https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps057.php
- Guzik: David speaks of his enemies' fall "with the anticipation of faith," before it had happened. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/
- Matthew Henry: their mischief came back on themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/57-5.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** Ellicott says the verb in "my soul is bowed down" is transitive everywhere else; the LXX and Vulgate read "they have pressed down my soul." He thinks the original parallel lines are now beyond recovery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/57.htm
- Bible.org calls the verse a typical Old Testament "reversal": enemies are caught in their own schemes. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21556

**v. 7**
- **Traditional:** Spurgeon: you'd expect "my heart is fluttered," but he is calm and resolute. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/57-7.htm
- Barnes: the Hebrew word means firm and upright, and repeating it shows his trust did not waver at all. Same URL.
- Maclaren: in Hebrew, "heart" includes will and thought as well as feelings. A fixed heart means steady resolve, not faith "by fits and starts." Same URL.
- Guzik: the psalm opened with two cries for mercy and now gives two statements of firmness. Morgan: "Fixity of heart is the secret of songs." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/

**v. 8**
- **"My glory":** Commentators disagree on what this means.
  - Poole and Gill: the tongue. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/57-8.htm
  - Pulpit: the soul (compare Ps 16:9; 30:12). Same URL.
  - Barnes: all his noblest powers. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/psalms/57-8.html
  - Clarke: one manuscript and the Syriac read "my harp," which he thinks is the original. Otherwise he takes it as David's skill in music. Same URL.
  - Bible.org: the Hebrew can mean "liver," that is, the inner self. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21556
- **"Awaken the dawn":**
  - Ellicott prefers "I will rouse the dawn." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/57.htm
  - JFB: a poetic way of showing zeal. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_057.cfm
  - Barnes: a general habit of giving the early morning to praise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/57-8.htm
  - The Biblical Illustrator: instead of the dawn waking David, he would wake it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-57.html
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon says a prepared heart wakes up a sleepy body, and that faith sings a victory song before the victory. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps057.php
- Clarke records a rabbinic legend of a harp by David's bed that played in the north wind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/

**v. 9**
- **Traditional:** Spurgeon sees a "missionary spirit" that wants the nations (Gentiles) to hear God's praise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-57.html
- Kidner notes that Paul quotes similar words (via Ps 18:49) in Romans 15:9 as a prophecy that had to be fulfilled. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/
- Matthew Henry: David still praises God among the nations through his psalms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/57-7.htm

**v. 10**
- **Traditional:** A Cambridge note points out that these are the same qualities sent to rescue him in v. 3, now shown victorious, and that the wording is close to Ps 36:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/57-10.htm
- Tholuck (quoted by Spurgeon): a thankful heart in a dark cave sees God's mercy as a huge ocean. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/
- Bible.org: the Hebrew word in the BSB's "loving devotion" (*chesed*) is often translated "steadfast love" or "covenant loyalty." https://biblehub.com/psalms/57.htm
- **Christ-centred reading:** Horne says the resurrection, foreshadowed by David's escape from Saul, made heaven praise God's mercy and truth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/

**v. 11**
- **Traditional:** Guzik: the refrain comes back for emphasis, while David's situation still hadn't really improved. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-57/
- Clarke and Ellicott both note that vv. 7–11 reappear, nearly word for word, as Ps 108:1–5. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/psalms/57-8.html

**Whole psalm: reading it as about Christ**
- Spurgeon's collection notes that "mystically" the psalm can be read of Christ, attacked by enemies both spiritual and earthly. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps057.cfm
- Augustine reads the whole psalm as Christ's Passion and resurrection, spoken by the "whole Christ," head and members. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801057.htm
